title: Azure DevOps ALM for a Governed Agent Factory
author: Sagar Rangi
contentRaw:
Introduction

Azure DevOps application lifecycle management automates how Power Platform solutions move from development to testing and production. The pipeline stores the release process as code, creates a managed solution artifact once, and promotes that same artifact through controlled stages.

For an Agent Factory, this matters because agents, flows, actions, connectors, and supporting Dataverse components must move together under repeatable governance. Separate environment identities, explicit access, deployment history, and a production approval reduce configuration drift and create an auditable release path.

Step by Step Configuration

Step 1 Create the Azure DevOps organization and private project

Open Azure DevOps, select New organization, and complete the organization wizard with a unique name and region. This implementation uses AF-PILOT-AZDO as the governed engineering boundary for the Agent Factory release path.

Sign in to Azure DevOps with the account that will administer the lab. Select Create new organization, enter AF-PILOT-AZDO, choose the appropriate hosting region, and continue.

Create AF-PILOT-ALM, add a short purpose statement, and set Visibility to Private before selecting Create. A private project keeps repositories, pipelines, service connections, and deployment history limited to explicitly authorized users and groups.

Step 2 Install Microsoft Power Platform Build Tools

Open the Visual Studio Marketplace page for Microsoft Power Platform Build Tools and select Get it free. Choose AF-PILOT-AZDO when the installation page asks which organization should receive the extension.

From Organization settings, open Extensions and select Browse marketplace. Search for Microsoft Power Platform Build Tools and open the Microsoft listing.

Select Get it free and install the extension into AF-PILOT-AZDO. Return to the Installed tab and confirm that Power Platform Build Tools appears as Active before creating the release pipeline.

Return to Azure DevOps Organization settings, open Extensions, and check the Installed tab. The extension should appear as Active before you create or run a pipeline that uses Power Platform tasks.

Step 3 Create the deployment identity

In Microsoft Entra admin center, open App registrations and select New registration. A dedicated application separates pipeline automation from personal identities and provides one controlled identity for environment access.

Enter APP-AF-AzureDevOps-ALM, select Accounts in this organizational directory only, and leave Redirect URI empty. Select Register; no client secret is required because authentication will use workload identity federation.

Step 4 Create one passwordless connection for each environment

In AF-PILOT-ALM Project settings, open Service connections and select New service connection. Create PP-AF-DEV-WIF, PP-AF-TEST-WIF, and PP-AF-PROD-WIF so every stage authenticates to only its matching Power Platform environment.

Repeat this workflow to create one workload-identity service connection for each environment: PP-AF-DEV-WIF, PP-AF-TEST-WIF, and PP-AF-PROD-WIF. Each connection must use the Dataverse URL of its matching environment.

For DEV, select Power Platform and Workload Identity federation. Enter the DEV Dataverse URL, the application client ID and tenant ID recorded in Step 3, name the connection PP-AF-DEV-WIF, and keep Grant access permission to all pipelines cleared.

Repeat the same configuration for TEST, changing only the Server URL and service connection name. This prevents a TEST deployment task from silently authenticating against DEV or PROD.

Repeat once more for PROD using the production Dataverse URL and PP-AF-PROD-WIF. Keep broad pipeline access disabled; authorize only the release pipeline when Azure DevOps requests permission on its first run.

For a manually configured Entra application, Azure DevOps supplies the issuer and subject values for each workload-identity service connection. Use those values to add one federated credential per environment to APP-AF-AzureDevOps-ALM. No client secret is required.

Step 5 Add the application user to DEV TEST and PROD

In each Power Platform environment, add APP-AF-AzureDevOps-ALM as an application user in the root business unit. System Administrator was used for this pilot to support complete solution deployment; production implementations should validate and reduce privileges where practical.

Step 6 Create the TEST and PROD deployment environments

Create Azure DevOps environment resources named AF-PILOT-TEST and AF-PILOT-PROD. These objects hold deployment history and provide the policy boundary used by approvals and checks.

The names match the existing Power Platform environments to keep the release path easy to understand. No change is made to the existing Power Platform Pipelines host or stages.

From Pipelines, open Environments and select New environment. Enter AF-PILOT-TEST, keep Resource set to None, and create the environment. Repeat the process for AF-PILOT-PROD.

Step 7 Require approval before PROD

Open AF-PILOT-TEST, select Approvals and checks, and add an approval check for validation releases. Repeat the same configuration in AF-PILOT-PROD. A production implementation should use an independent approver group and normally prevent self-approval.

Repeat the check on AF-PILOT-PROD. The approval belongs to the Azure DevOps environment, so a change to the YAML file cannot remove the production gate.

Step 8 Create the YAML pipeline

Open Pipelines and select New pipeline. Choose Azure Repos Git because the YAML file is stored in the project repository. The wizard links the pipeline definition to the existing source-controlled release file.

Select the AF-PILOT-ALM repository, choose Existing Azure Pipelines YAML file, select the main branch and /azure-pipelines.yml, and continue to the review page. Azure DevOps created this default Git repository when the AF-PILOT-ALM project was provisioned.

Store the YAML definition in the default repository

The YAML validates each connection, sets a release version, exports AF_Pilot_Agent as a managed solution, and publishes one immutable artifact. TEST and PROD both import that exact ZIP rather than creating separate packages.

The pilot uses trigger none so releases start manually. Branch policies and pull-request validation can be added later without changing the deployment model.

Step 9 Run the pipeline and authorize only required resources

Open Pipelines, choose AF-PILOT-ALM, and select Run pipeline. Confirm the main branch before starting the run. On the first execution, explicitly permit this pipeline to use each service connection and Azure DevOps environment instead of granting access to every pipeline.

The DEV stage validates its passwordless connection, sets the release version, exports AF_Pilot_Agent as a managed solution, and publishes the ZIP as the release artifact. The TEST stage then downloads and imports that exact artifact.

After TEST succeeds, Azure DevOps pauses at the protected PROD environment. The approval decision is recorded in the run before the production import task can start.

Step 10 Review TEST and approve the production release

After TEST succeeds, review the artifact and deployment result, then approve the AF-PILOT-PROD check. The production job cannot request an agent or import the solution until this independent resource check passes.

Validation

The end-to-end validation confirmed that the passwordless identity authenticated in all three environments, DEV exported a managed solution, and Azure DevOps published one release artifact. The same artifact imported into TEST before the production checkpoint became available.

The production environment check recorded the approval, after which the final deployment job completed. Pipeline history now links the source commit, artifact, approver decision, and environment deployments in one audit trail.

The PROD solution list confirms that the managed AF Pilot Agent solution was updated by the pipeline, completing the functional validation beyond the Azure DevOps status alone.

Why This Is Relevant for Agent Factory

  • Repeatability: A versioned YAML process applies the same release logic to every governed agent solution.
  • Artifact integrity: TEST and PROD receive the same managed ZIP, reducing environment drift.
  • Identity isolation: Passwordless service connections separate DEV, TEST, and PROD access.
  • Production control: An environment-owned approval prevents a YAML edit from bypassing the release decision.
  • Auditability: Commits, artifacts, approvals, and deployments remain linked in Azure DevOps history.

Conclusion

Azure DevOps provides a production-ready ALM option when organizations need source-controlled pipelines, reusable templates, enterprise approvals, and deeper integration with engineering workflows. A governed design should promote one managed artifact, use environment-scoped identities, and keep production approval outside the YAML file. Power Platform Pipelines can remain available alongside this approach, allowing each organization to choose the release path that fits its operating model.
